name: Moral Luck
statement: We praise and blame people for things partly beyond their control, which seems to violate a basic principle.
statementAccent: for things partly beyond their control
meaning: Moral luck is a problem in moral philosophy that arises when an agent is morally judged, praised or blamed, for an action or its outcomes even though a significant aspect of what they are judged for was due to factors beyond their control, that is, to luck. The topic was named and framed in a famous 1976 exchange between the philosophers Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, who each published a paper titled Moral Luck. The problem is that this common practice of moral judgment conflicts with a deeply intuitive principle, the control principle, according to which we are morally assessable only for what is within our control, and cannot be morally judged for what is not our fault or not up to us. Yet in practice we constantly assess people for things shaped by luck, so the control principle and our actual moral practice pull against each other, creating a paradox. Nagel identified four kinds of moral luck: resultant luck, in how one's actions turn out; circumstantial luck, in the situations one happens to face; constitutive luck, in the character and temperament one has but did not choose; and causal luck, in how one is determined by prior circumstances. Moral luck is a central problem in the theory of moral responsibility, bearing on blame, desert, free will, and the law.
mechanism: Moral luck names the tension between two things we are strongly inclined to accept. On one side is the control principle: the intuition that we are morally assessable only to the extent that what we are assessed for depends on factors under our control, so that two people who differ only in ways beyond their control should not be judged differently. On the other side is our actual moral practice, which routinely does judge people differently on the basis of factors beyond their control. Where these clash, moral luck arises. Nagel distinguished four kinds. Resultant luck is luck in the way things turn out, the consequences of one's actions: a drunk driver who happens to kill a pedestrian who runs into the road is blamed and punished far more severely than an equally drunk driver who happens to arrive home safely, though the difference is luck. Circumstantial luck is luck in the circumstances one finds oneself in, as when a person becomes a collaborator under a brutal regime while someone of identical character, who happened to emigrate, is never tested. Constitutive luck is luck in one's own character, temperament, and dispositions, which one did not choose. And causal luck is luck in how one is determined by antecedent circumstances, connecting the problem to the free will debate. In each case, factors beyond the agent's control shape the moral judgment we make, threatening to shrink the domain of genuine moral responsibility.

examples.text: Two identically drunk drivers differ only by luck when one hits a child and faces manslaughter while the other gets home safely.
Nagel distinguished resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, and causal moral luck, each involving factors beyond the agent's control.
A person might collaborate under a brutal regime while an identical person who emigrated is never put to the test, a matter of luck.

whyItMatters: Moral luck is a major problem in ethics and the theory of moral responsibility, because it exposes a deep and unresolved tension in our moral thinking. On the one hand, we firmly believe that people should be judged only for what is within their control; on the other, we constantly praise and blame them for outcomes, circumstances, and even character traits that are substantially matters of luck. By naming and analyzing this tension, Williams and Nagel showed that our ordinary moral practice may rest on a principle it cannot consistently honor, and Nagel argued that pressing the control principle threatens to shrink the domain of genuine moral responsibility almost to nothing, since so much about us and our actions is ultimately beyond our control. The problem bears directly on blame, praise, and desert, on the justification of legal punishment, where results-based sentencing treats the drunk driver who kills more harshly than the one who does not, and on the free will debate, since causal luck connects it to determinism. Moral luck forces reflection on the foundations of moral judgment itself. As the problem of holding people responsible for what luck partly determines, it is a central and disquieting puzzle in moral philosophy.

recognize the clash between the control principle and our practice across resultant, circumstantial, constitutive, and causal luck.

limits: Moral luck is a genuine problem rather than a settled doctrine, and philosophers respond to it in different ways rather than agreeing on a solution. Some deny that there is any real moral luck, holding that we should revise our practices to conform to the control principle, so that, for instance, the successful and the unsuccessful drunk driver are equally blameworthy and only our reactive practices differ. Others accept moral luck and reject or qualify the control principle, holding that moral assessment legitimately tracks outcomes, circumstances, and character. Still others try to locate a core of responsibility that luck does not touch. Because the four kinds of luck differ, a response adequate to one, such as resultant luck, may not settle another, such as constitutive or causal luck, and causal luck in particular merges into the intractable free will problem. So moral luck robustly exposes the tension between the control principle and our moral practice, understood as an unresolved problem admitting several competing responses rather than a fixed conclusion.
misreadings: Moral luck is not the claim that morality is simply a matter of luck; it names a tension between the control principle and our practice of judging people for what luck partly determines. It does not by itself tell us which side to give up, since some philosophers reject moral luck to save the control principle while others accept it and revise the principle. And its four kinds are distinct, so solving one does not solve all, so treating moral luck as reducing morality to chance, as delivering a settled verdict, or as a single uniform problem, misreads an unresolved puzzle in the theory of responsibility.
origin: A problem in moral philosophy named and framed in a 1976 exchange between Bernard Williams and Thomas Nagel, concerning the moral assessment of agents for actions and outcomes partly beyond their control.
